title: 67 (Six Seven)
blurb: Six... seven! The two numbers that broke a generation. Born from a Skrilla track and turbocharged by basketball edits, 67 became Gen Alpha's inside joke — a call-and-response chant with hand gestures, screamed in classrooms worldwide until teachers begged for mercy. It means nothing. It means everything. Ask a kid what 67 means and watch them short-circuit trying to explain. Peak brainrot, perfectly preserved.
origin: From Skrilla's 'Doot Doot (6 7)', amplified by basketball edits into a global Gen Alpha chant.

blurb: 20 + 20 + 20 + 7 = 67. The arithmetic proof that the internet's favorite number sequence is, in fact, correct. This variant turned the 67 chant into a math lesson nobody asked for, and it spread through classrooms exactly as fast as you'd expect. Play it to explain the meme, to annoy a teacher, or to settle the world's dumbest equation once and for all.
origin: A math-variant riff on the viral 67 brainrot chant.

title: Tung Tung Tung Sahur
blurb: TUNG TUNG TUNG TUNG TUNG SAHUR — the hypnotic drum chant from Indonesia's sahur wake-up tradition, transformed by the internet into one of the defining Italian brainrot characters. The rhythm is relentless, the AI-generated wooden creature is unsettling, and together they colonized every For You page on Earth. If you've heard it once, it's already living in your head rent-free.
origin: From Indonesian sahur drum-calling tradition; became a cornerstone Italian brainrot character.

title: Tralalero Tralala
blurb: Tralalero Tralala — the three-legged shark in Nike sneakers, patriarch of the entire Italian brainrot universe. The absurd Italian voiceover launched a thousand AI-generated creatures and one of the strangest meme movements in internet history. Nobody can explain why a shark in trainers conquered global youth culture, but the audio is undeniable proof that it did.
origin: The founding character of the Italian brainrot meme wave.

title: Sigma Boy
blurb: Sigma boy, sigma boy — the Russian pop earworm that turned 'sigma' from ironic manosphere slang into a playground anthem. The song is genuinely catchy, which made it unstoppable: it charted internationally purely on meme momentum. Play it to summon every child within a hundred metres, or to acknowledge someone displaying certified sigma behaviour.
origin: The viral Russian pop song by Betsy and Maria Yankovskaya that took over TikTok.

title: Thick of It (KSI)
blurb: 'In the thick of it, everybody knows...' — KSI's track that became the internet's most remixed hook, spawning an entire genre of edits where the lyrics get replaced with increasingly unhinged nonsense. The original is the foundation; every brainrot variant builds on it. Play it as a flex, a bit, or the opening statement of a rap battle nobody agreed to.
origin: From KSI's 'Thick of It' — the internet's most-remixed hook.

title: Thick of It (Brainrot Version)
blurb: The brainrot edition of Thick of It — the version where the lyrics have been replaced by pure meme vocabulary and the whole thing has been deep-fried past recognition. This is what happens when a hit song meets the internet's blender: skibidi, sigma, and gyatt all somehow present. The original made the charts; this one made the classroom unusable.
origin: The brainrot-lyric remix of KSI's Thick of It.

title: Brainrot Rap
blurb: The brainrot rap — every Gen Alpha buzzword compressed into a single track. Skibidi, gyatt, rizz, sigma, fanum tax, Ohio: the whole lexicon, delivered with unearned confidence over a beat. It's simultaneously a parody and a genuine artifact of the era. Play it for anyone who wants to understand modern youth slang, then apologise to them afterwards.
origin: A viral track cataloguing the entire Gen Alpha brainrot vocabulary.

title: Labubu Funk
blurb: Labubu funk — the beat that soundtracked the great Labubu takeover, when a fanged little plush monster became the most fought-over collectible on the planet. Queues, resales, celebrity sightings, and a genuinely unhinged fandom, all set to this. Play it in tribute to whatever you're currently overpaying for. The teeth are part of the appeal.
origin: The funk track attached to the viral Labubu collectible craze.

title: Steve's Lava Chicken
blurb: 'Steve's lava chicken, spicy!' — Jack Black's fourteen-second Minecraft Movie song that charted internationally and became the most quoted thing in any playground. It's absurdly short, absurdly catchy, and absurdly successful: an actual charting single about chicken cooked in lava. Play it and watch every child in earshot complete the lyric automatically.
origin: Jack Black's viral song from A Minecraft Movie (2025).

title: Hawk Tuah
blurb: Hawk tuah — the street-interview answer that turned an anonymous woman into a global phenomenon overnight, spawning merch, podcasts, and one of the fastest fame cycles the internet has produced. The delivery is what sold it: complete confidence, zero hesitation. A perfect case study in how three syllables can become an entire cultural moment.
origin: From the 2024 Nashville street interview that became an instant global meme.

title: Ronaldo SIUUU
blurb: SIUUUU — Cristiano Ronaldo's celebration cry, the most imitated sound in world football. Every schoolyard, every FIFA lobby, every kid who has ever jumped and spun after scoring anything. It's not a word; it's a declaration of superiority. Play it after any victory, no matter how small, and land the jump properly.
origin: Cristiano Ronaldo's iconic 'SIUUU' goal celebration.

title: No (Verity)
blurb: Verity's 'No' — the flat refusal from the yellow companion who became Minecraft horror's breakout star. What makes it unsettling is the total lack of emotion: Verity isn't angry, isn't negotiating, just declining. ThatMob's series made this little voice genuinely ominous, and the internet adopted it as the coldest possible rejection sound.
origin: From ThatMob's Verity Minecraft horror series.

title: Verity Greeting
blurb: Verity's greeting — the friendly hello that opens the Minecraft horror series everyone is currently obsessed with. It sounds welcoming. It is not welcoming. That gap between the cheerful delivery and everything that follows is exactly why the Verity phenomenon works, and why this clip hits so much harder once you know the story.
origin: The introduction greeting from the Verity Minecraft horror series.

title: Verity: Something Is Coming
blurb: 'Something is coming.' — Verity's warning line, delivered in that unnervingly calm register that made the series a phenomenon. It's the perfect dread sound: no scream, no music sting, just a quiet statement of fact about something you cannot see yet. Use it for ominous foreshadowing, or to ruin a friend's evening.
origin: A warning line from the Verity Minecraft horror series.

title: I Like Ya Cut G
blurb: 'I like ya cut, G!' — followed immediately by a slap to the back of a freshly-cut head. The compliment-then-assault format became one of the internet's most reliable prank templates, and this audio is the trigger. Play it near anyone with a new haircut and watch them flinch defensively. The compliment is sincere. The slap is mandatory.
origin: From the viral haircut-slap prank format.

title: Let Him Cook
blurb: 'Let him cook!' — the internet's plea to not interrupt someone mid-brilliance. Whether the person is actually cooking or catastrophically failing is beside the point; the phrase demands you find out. It became the default hype comment on everything from gameplay to unhinged Twitter threads. Sometimes he was, in fact, not cooking. We let him anyway.
origin: The viral 'let him cook' hype phrase from streaming and sports culture.

title: Daddy Chill
blurb: 'What the hell is even that? DADDY CHILL' — the legendary line from an amateur web series that the internet elevated to scripture. The delivery is so wooden, so committed, and so completely unbothered by acting that it looped its way into permanent meme canon. Play it when someone needs to calm down immediately and inexplicably.
origin: From the viral 'What the hell is even that?' web-series clip.

title: GOO GOO GA GA
blurb: GOO GOO GA GA — baby talk deployed as a weapon. The internet uses it to declare someone is being childish, to mock a bad take into oblivion, or simply to derail a serious conversation with maximum efficiency. It's the verbal equivalent of a pacifier being thrown at someone's argument. Devastating, and technically pre-verbal.
origin: The viral baby-talk mockery sound.

title: Where Are You Going?
blurb: 'Where are you going?' — asked with the particular menace of someone who already knows you have nowhere to be. It's the audio for interceptions: catching someone sneaking off, spotting a friend leaving the party early, or a cat halfway out the window. The question is rhetorical. You're not going anywhere.
origin: A viral confrontational-question clip.

title: Stop, Don't Talk to Me
blurb: 'Stop, don't talk to me' — the sung dismissal that ends conversations with rhythm. Being rejected is one thing; being rejected melodically is another. TikTok made it the soundtrack for shutting down unwanted approaches, group-chat drama, and anyone starting a sentence with 'actually'. Musical, final, and impossible to argue with.
origin: A viral sung dismissal from TikTok.

title: English or Spanish?
blurb: 'English or Spanish?' — the interrogation that became a whole genre. Originating from a viral prank format, it's now the internet's favourite way to demand answers: you get two options, both wrong, and no time to think. Play it before asking anyone anything. The pressure is the point.
origin: From the viral 'English or Spanish' interrogation prank format.

title: MrBeast Rizz
blurb: MrBeast rizz — the clip where the world's biggest YouTuber demonstrates charisma with the intensity of a man giving away an island. Whether it's genuine or catastrophic is exactly the debate that made it a meme. Play it during any confident approach, ideally while offering someone $10,000 to do something inadvisable.
origin: A viral clip of MrBeast's charisma, endlessly debated online.

title: SIKE
blurb: SIKE! — the reversal that invalidates everything said before it. It's the internet's undo button for sincerity: compliment someone, build them up, then sike. Cruel? Yes. Effective? Devastatingly. The word predates the internet by decades and has never once lost its power to make someone feel briefly, wonderfully foolish.
origin: The classic 'sike' reversal, meme-canonised.

title: Ice Spice Son
blurb: The Ice Spice 'son' clip — delivered with the bored authority of someone who has already won the exchange. It became a go-to reaction for putting people in their place with minimum effort. No shouting, no argument, just one syllable that reframes the entire conversation and establishes a very clear hierarchy.
origin: A viral Ice Spice interview moment adopted as a dismissal.

title: Tiki Tiki
blurb: Tiki tiki — a nonsense chant with a rhythm engineered to lodge itself permanently in your auditory cortex. It means nothing, does nothing, and cannot be evicted. TikTok specialises in this genre: sounds that spread purely because they're fun to repeat. Resistance is optional and ineffective.
origin: A viral nonsense chant from TikTok.

title: I Live With Roaches
blurb: 'I live with roaches' — a confession delivered with such matter-of-fact calm that it became a meme about accepting your circumstances. The internet adopted it for admitting to any unglamorous truth: the state of your flat, your finances, your standards. Honesty this bleak circles back around to being genuinely funny.
origin: A viral deadpan confession clip.

title: Oi Oi Oi
blurb: OI OI OI — the chant that turns any group into a crowd. It's football-terrace energy compressed into two seconds, deployable at parties, in Discord calls, and anywhere collective enthusiasm needs igniting. The internet's most efficient hype primer. Say it once and someone will always answer.
origin: A viral crowd-chant sound.

title: Funky Ehh
blurb: The Funky Ehh sound — a groove-plus-grunt combination that soundtracked a wave of dance edits and made 'ehh' a rhythmic instrument. It's silly, it's danceable, and it demonstrates the internet's core talent: taking a meaningless vocal noise and building an entire trend on top of it.
origin: A viral dance-edit sound built around a rhythmic 'ehh'.

title: White Tee Rizz
blurb: White tee rizz — proof that charisma requires no wardrobe budget. The clip celebrates the specific confidence of someone pulling everything off in a plain white t-shirt, which the internet decided is the ultimate flex. Play it for anyone whose entire aesthetic is 'clean basics and unshakeable self-belief'.
origin: A viral rizz clip celebrating minimal-outfit confidence.

title: That's Too Easy (LeBron)
blurb: 'That's too easy.' — LeBron James dismissing a challenge that other people find difficult. It's the ultimate low-effort flex: no celebration, no gloating, just a statement of fact about the gap in skill. Play it after solving something trivially, or ironically after barely surviving something that was in fact extremely hard.
origin: LeBron James's viral 'that's too easy' dismissal.

title: Ice Cream Truck (Baby Boo)
blurb: The ice cream truck jingle — the sound that has commanded children to run since the invention of the freezer. Its tinny, slightly-off melody is universally recognised and mildly ominous when heard at the wrong hour. Play it to trigger childhood Pavlovian responses in adults, or to announce that the treats have arrived.
origin: The classic ice cream truck jingle, viral as a nostalgia trigger.

title: Ding Dong Eat It Up
blurb: Ding dong, eat it up — the chaotic little food chant that TikTok attached to snacks, meals, and general consumption. It has the energy of someone dancing in front of an open fridge at midnight. Play it when food arrives, when the fridge calls, or when your self-control has clocked off for the day.
origin: A viral food-related TikTok chant.

title: VERY LOUD FAHHH
blurb: VERY LOUD FAHHH — the most-played sound on entire soundboards, and a legitimate hearing hazard. The 'fahh' scream is meme culture's purest expression of shock, and this version removes any volume ceiling. It's the sound for jump scares, sudden realisations, and destroying the audio of anyone who trusted you with an unmuted mic.
origin: The maximum-volume edition of the viral 'fahh' scream.

title: Fahhh
blurb: The original 'fahhh' — the strangled scream that became one of the internet's most-searched sounds. It's shock, panic, and disbelief compressed into a single syllable that isn't quite a word. Play it when something goes wrong at speed. This is the standard-volume version, for when you still want your friends to keep their hearing.
origin: The viral 'fahh' shock scream.

title: I Got This... FAHHHHH
blurb: 'I got this' — immediately followed by FAHHHHH. The complete arc of overconfidence meeting reality, in two seconds. It's the audio biography of every plan that seemed fine until it wasn't. Play it over anything that begins with certainty and ends in disaster, which is most things.
origin: The viral confidence-then-catastrophe 'fahh' clip.

title: Samsung Notification
blurb: The Samsung notification — the Android world's answer to the iPhone ping, and instantly recognisable to roughly a billion people. It carries the same reflex power: play it in a room and every Galaxy owner reaches for their pocket. Essential for the notification-prank arsenal, and a fair-and-balanced companion to our iPhone sound.
origin: Samsung's default notification tone.

title: Samsung Whistle
blurb: The Samsung Whistle — the cheerful two-note whistle that served as Galaxy's signature ringtone for years. It's one of the most recognisable mobile sounds ever shipped, and it works beautifully as a prank: nobody can hear it without checking. Nostalgic for Android veterans, mildly infuriating for everyone else.
origin: Samsung's classic 'Whistle' ringtone.

title: WhatsApp Notification
blurb: The WhatsApp notification — quite possibly the most-heard message alert on the planet, given the app's three billion users. Outside the US especially, this tiny sound governs daily life: family groups, work chats, the neighbour asking about the bins. Play it anywhere in the world and watch heads turn simultaneously.
origin: WhatsApp's default message notification.

title: Snapchat Notification
blurb: The Snapchat notification — the alert that means your streak is safe, or someone screenshotted something they shouldn't have. It carries a specific teenage urgency no other notification matches. Play it near anyone under twenty-five and observe the immediate panic-check. Streak maintenance is not optional.
origin: Snapchat's notification alert.

title: iPhone Camera Shutter
blurb: The iPhone camera shutter — the fake mechanical click Apple added so phones couldn't take photos silently. It's now the universal sound of being photographed, wanted or otherwise. Use it in edits for photo moments, or play it behind someone to convince them they've just been captured mid-embarrassment.
origin: Apple's simulated camera shutter click.

title: iPhone Sent Message
blurb: The iPhone sent-message swoosh — the sound of a text leaving your hands forever. It's the audio of commitment: the moment the message becomes unrecallable and the regret window opens. Pair it with our iPhone notification for the full conversational cycle, or play it right after someone says something they shouldn't have.
origin: Apple's message-sent swoosh.

title: FaceTime Connect
blurb: The FaceTime connect sound — the chirp that means the call has gone through and your camera is now, regrettably, live. It's the companion to our FaceTime hang-up: one opens the ordeal, the other ends it. Play it in edits to start a call scene, or to make someone check whether their camera is on. It probably is.
origin: Apple's FaceTime call-connect sound.

title: Amber Alert
blurb: The Amber Alert tone — the emergency broadcast screech that overrides every phone setting and every conversation. It's designed to be impossible to ignore, which makes it the most effective prank sound in existence and the most alarming. Every phone in a room will be checked instantly. Use sparingly; this one genuinely startles people.
origin: The emergency alert tone used for Amber Alerts.

title: Tornado Warning
blurb: The tornado warning siren — the rising civil-defence wail that means take shelter immediately. It's the most primal alarm in the American soundscape, and outside of an actual emergency it makes an exceptionally effective prank. Also excellent for edits where a situation escalates from bad to meteorological.
origin: The civil-defence tornado warning siren.

title: New Year's Ball Drop Countdown
blurb: Ten, nine, eight... the Times Square ball-drop countdown, complete with crowd. It's the most collectively-experienced countdown on Earth, and it works for any moment that deserves ceremony: a launch, a reveal, a microwave finishing. Play it and watch everyone in the room instinctively join in around 'three'.
origin: The Times Square New Year's Eve countdown.

title: Minecraft XP
blurb: The Minecraft XP orb sound — that satisfying bubbling collection noise as experience streams into you. It's one of gaming's most quietly perfect audio rewards: soft, plentiful, and endlessly re-triggerable. Play it whenever you learn something, finish a task, or want to make any mundane achievement feel like progress toward enchanting.
origin: The experience-orb collection sound from Minecraft.

title: Victory Royale (Fortnite)
blurb: The Victory Royale music — the triumphant sting that means you outlived ninety-nine other people. For an entire generation this is what winning sounds like. Play it after any victory, however unearned: parking well, winning an argument, being the last person awake. Number one Victory Royale energy applies universally.
origin: The win music from Fortnite (Epic Games).

title: Shield Potion (Fortnite)
blurb: The Fortnite shield potion glug — the gulping sound of drinking blue liquid while being shot at. It's one of the most recognisable sounds in modern gaming, and it doubles as the internet's audio for chugging anything. Play it while drinking, before entering a difficult conversation, or any time you need fifty extra shield.
origin: The shield-potion drinking sound from Fortnite.

title: Pump Shotgun (Fortnite)
blurb: The Fortnite pump shotgun blast — the single most decisive sound in the game. One shot, one outcome, no discussion. Its distinctive crack is burned into millions of players' memories, usually as the last thing they heard. Play it to end arguments, edits, or anything else that needs immediate closure.
origin: The pump shotgun fire sound from Fortnite.

title: Fortnite Default Dance
blurb: The Default Dance music — Fortnite's most disrespectful emote, performed over defeated opponents worldwide. It transcended the game entirely to become the universal celebration of humiliating someone. Play it after any victory where rubbing it in is the whole point. The dance is optional; the disrespect is not.
origin: The music from Fortnite's Default Dance emote.

title: Nice Throw (Wii Sports)
blurb: 'Nice throw!' — Wii Sports bowling's relentlessly supportive announcer, praising you regardless of the actual result. The Wii-era optimism is unmatched: this man believes in you completely and has never once been discouraging. Play it for genuine successes, or for the ironic joy of being complimented on something that went badly.
origin: The bowling announcer from Wii Sports (Nintendo, 2006).

title: Wii Sports Theme
blurb: The Wii Sports theme — the jaunty piano tune that opened millions of family evenings in 2007. It is pure distilled nostalgia: hearing it summons memories of wrist straps, broken TVs, and grandmothers unexpectedly dominating at bowling. One of the most beloved video game themes ever written, for reasons that have nothing to do with the game.
origin: The main theme from Wii Sports (Nintendo, 2006).

title: Wii Sports Aww
blurb: The Wii Sports 'aww' — the crowd's gentle disappointment when you gutter the ball or miss the shot. It's the kindest failure sound ever programmed: nobody's angry, everyone's just a little sad for you. Play it for near-misses, honest attempts, and moments that deserve sympathy rather than mockery.
origin: The crowd's disappointed 'aww' from Wii Sports.

title: Undertale Intro Boom
blurb: The Undertale intro boom — the deep, ominous hit that opens one of gaming's most beloved stories. Toby Fox's sound design does a lot with very little, and this single impact sets the entire tone. Play it before dramatic reveals, or to give any announcement the weight of a genocide-route ending.
origin: The intro impact from Undertale (Toby Fox).

title: Super Mario Boh Boh
blurb: The Mario 'boh boh' — one of the plumber's stranger vocalisations, isolated and looped until it stopped making sense entirely. Mario has produced a lot of noises across four decades, and the internet has found comedy in most of them. This one is pure nonsense syllables from gaming's most famous voice. Boh boh.
origin: A vocal clip from the Super Mario series.

title: Russian Minecraft Kid Screaming
blurb: The Russian Minecraft kid scream — an eruption of pure unfiltered rage from a child whose base was almost certainly griefed. It's the sound of gaming taken extremely seriously by someone very small. Play it for rage-quit moments, or as a warning about what happens when you touch someone else's chests.
origin: A viral clip of a young Minecraft player screaming.

title: AH It's Coming Out (Golden Freddy)
blurb: The Golden Freddy edition of the panicked 'AH, IT'S COMING OUT' clip — FNAF's most mysterious animatronic crossed with one of the internet's most chaotic screams. It's exactly the kind of unhinged crossover the FNAF fandom produces at industrial scale. Genuinely startling, entirely unserious, and beloved by both communities.
origin: A FNAF fandom remix combining Golden Freddy with a viral panic clip.

title: Michael Don't Leave Me Here
blurb: 'MICHAEL, DON'T LEAVE ME HERE!' — one of FNAF lore's most emotionally devastating lines, screamed with genuine desperation. The series buries real tragedy under its jump scares, and this clip is where the mask slips. Play it dramatically when someone leaves a Discord call, or sincerely if you actually understand the lore.
origin: A line from Five Nights at Freddy's lore, adopted by the fandom.

title: Stelio Kontos
blurb: STELIO KONTOS — the theme of Dexter's Laboratory's most menacing character, a man whose entire personality is intimidation. The music is so dramatically over-the-top for a children's cartoon that the internet adopted it as universal approach music. Play it when someone walks in with bad intentions and worse energy.
origin: The theme of Stelio Kontos from Dexter's Laboratory.

title: Slap
blurb: A clean, crisp slap — the sharp smack that punctuates shock, discipline, and comedic violence. It's one of editing's most-used impacts because it works on everything: reality checks, punchlines, and the moment someone says something that deserves consequences. Sound designers have made cinema's slaps unrealistically loud for decades. We continue the tradition.
origin: A clean cinematic slap impact.

title: Pew
blurb: Pew. The most efficient onomatopoeia in existence — a tiny laser noise that everyone can make with their mouth and everyone finds funny. It's the sound of finger guns, imaginary blasters, and playful violence. Deploy it liberally; the pew has no wrong context and costs nothing emotionally.
origin: The classic cartoon laser 'pew'.

title: Clap Clap
blurb: Two deliberate claps — the most passive-aggressive applause available. It's not celebration; it's commentary. Use it for sarcastic congratulation, the beginning of a slow clap, or to acknowledge someone's achievement in the least enthusiastic way physically possible. Well done. Truly.
origin: Two isolated claps — sarcastic applause.

title: Hyper Realistic Knocking
blurb: Knocking so realistic it has ruined thousands of evenings. This is the elite tier of prank audio: play it through decent speakers and the listener will physically get up and check the door. Nobody is there. Nobody was ever there. Its entire reputation is built on how many people it has successfully fooled.
origin: A high-fidelity door-knock recording, famous as a prank sound.

title: Core Sound Effect
blurb: The 'core' sound — the transition sting from the aesthetic-core meme genre, where every possible mood was given a name and a moodboard. Cottagecore, weirdcore, corporate-core: the suffix conquered the internet, and this is its audio signature. Play it before revealing anyone's aesthetic, sincerely or otherwise.
origin: The transition sting from the '-core' aesthetic meme genre.

title: The Bluetooth Device Is Ready to Pair
blurb: 'The Bluetooth device is ready to pair.' — the flat robotic announcement that has interrupted more conversations than any other piece of consumer tech. It's aggressively unhelpful, weirdly loud, and instantly recognisable. Play it mid-sentence to derail someone entirely, or in edits about technology refusing to cooperate.
origin: The stock Bluetooth pairing voice prompt.

title: M e o w
blurb: A single perfect meow — the most demanding syllable in the animal kingdom. Cats produce this sound almost exclusively for humans, which makes every meow a targeted request. Play it to summon cat owners, punctuate cute moments, or communicate a need without specifying what it is. The cat knows what it did.
origin: A single clear cat meow.

blurb: 'What's nine plus ten?' 'Twenty-one.' The most famous incorrect arithmetic in internet history, and a founding text of Vine comedy. The confidence of the delivery is what immortalised it — the kid never wavered, never corrected, and accidentally created a decade-long meme. Still funny. Still wrong. Still twenty-one.
origin: From the legendary 2013 Vine — the internet's favourite wrong answer.

title: Oh No! Our Table! It's Broken
blurb: 'Oh no! Our table... it's broken!' — delivered with the emotional register of a war crime being discovered. The gap between the tragedy of the line reading and the triviality of a broken table is the entire joke, and it has sustained the meme for years. Deploy for minor property damage everywhere.
origin: From a viral clip of extremely dramatic furniture grief.

title: He Need Some Milk
blurb: 'HE NEED SOME MILK!' — shouted by a bystander at a viral moment of physical distress, and instantly canonised. It's the internet's prescription for anyone visibly struggling: not medical attention, not sympathy, milk. Play it when someone gets hurt, embarrassed, or generally requires dairy-based intervention.
origin: From the viral video where a bystander diagnoses the need for milk.

title: Pikachu Confused
blurb: Pikachu's confused noise — the audio companion to the surprised Pikachu face, one of the most-used reaction images ever made. It's the sound of shock at an entirely predictable outcome: the consequences you were warned about arriving exactly on schedule. Play it when someone acts shocked by their own decisions.
origin: The confused vocalisation behind the Surprised Pikachu meme.

title: Dumb Patrick
blurb: The Dumb Patrick sound — Bikini Bottom's most confidently unintelligent resident, in audio form. Patrick has spent decades being wrong with total conviction, which makes him the internet's patron saint of bad takes. Play it when someone says something so misguided it deserves a starfish's endorsement.
origin: Patrick Star's iconic dim-witted delivery from SpongeBob SquarePants.

title: Homer: Let the Barts Out
blurb: 'Let the Barts out!' — a Simpsons line that the internet extracted, isolated, and turned into pure absurdist nonsense. Out of context it means nothing; that's precisely why it works. The Simpsons has supplied meme material for thirty-five years and shows no sign of running dry. Release the Barts.
origin: An out-of-context line from The Simpsons.

title: McDonald's Ba Da Ba Ba Ba
blurb: Ba da ba ba ba — five notes that a billion people can identify instantly. McDonald's sonic logo is one of the most successful pieces of audio branding ever made, and the internet uses it whenever anything is 'lovin' it': good food, good news, questionable 3am decisions. Pairs perfectly with our fry timer beep.
origin: McDonald's 'I'm Lovin' It' sonic logo.

title: We Bring the Boom
blurb: 'We bring the boom' — a declaration of incoming chaos, delivered with total confidence. It's an announcement rather than a warning: whatever is about to happen has already been decided. Play it before entrances, plot twists, and any situation where the energy is about to change permanently.
origin: A viral hype declaration clip.

title: Rip My Granny
blurb: 'Rip my granny' — dark humour delivered with the timing of a stand-up routine. It belongs to the meme tradition of processing grief through absolute nonsense, which is either deeply healthy or deeply concerning depending on your therapist. The internet found it funny. The internet usually does.
origin: A viral dark-comedy clip.

title: Quandale Dingle Farted
blurb: 'Quandale Dingle farted' — a sentence that requires no further explanation and admits none. The Quandale saga generated hundreds of these absurd micro-narratives, each more committed to the bit than the last. Play it as a status update, an accusation, or a complete short story. Quandale did what he did.
origin: From the Quandale Dingle meme universe.

title: Anderdingus
blurb: Anderdingus — another entry in the internet's collection of names too stupid to be real and too funny to forget. It belongs to the same absurdist family as Quandale Dingle: characters who exist purely because their names are hilarious. Play it as a greeting, an insult, or an introduction to someone who deserves neither.
origin: A goofy-ahh-genre character name in the Quandale Dingle tradition.

title: Horse Noises
blurb: A horse in full vocal expression — neighing, snorting, and generally being the most dramatic animal on the farm. Horses are enormous and emotionally volatile, and they sound exactly like that. Play it for cowboy edits, unexpected arrivals, or any situation where the appropriate response is simply a horse.
origin: Classic horse neighing and snorting.
